sections.title: Cybersecurity Organization and Identity of the CySO
authoring_notes: CITATION CORRECTIONS applied against 33 CFR Part 101 Subpart F (current as of 8/25/2026). The source draft miscited three provisions.
1. 24/7 CySO availability was attributed to 101.625(b). That paragraph is 'Serving as CySO for Multiple Vessels'. The requirement is 101.620(b)(3). Both regulatory gaps reassigned.

2. The alternate CySO was attributed to 101.625(d). That paragraph is the 15-item CySO Responsibilities list. The alternate provision is in the 101.615 definition of Cybersecurity Officer. Gap reassigned.
3. The strengthened draft's list of the 12 knowledge areas did not match 101.625(e)(1)-(12). Replaced with the actual list.
Checklist ground truth for the three 101.620(b) items is inferred: the reveal lists no regulatory gap against them.

CITATION CORRECTION: subsection 1.4 asserted 24-hour COTP notification for a CySO change and paired it with the 30-day rule. 101.630(e)(4) sets two 96-hour clocks, one to notify and one to submit the amended portion, and 101.630(e)(2)'s 30 days does not govern this case. Both corrected.

blocks.text: Jordan Kim joined Maritime Enterprise Group in 2022 after eight years at Pacific Northwest Logistics, where he served as Senior IT Manager overseeing a 200-endpoint environment. Prior to that, Jordan spent three years at a managed security services provider (MSSP) supporting clients in the transportation and logistics sector. Jordan holds CISSP and GICSP certifications and has completed vendor-specific training from Palo Alto Networks, Splunk, and Siemens.

Jordan was selected for the CySO role based on a competitive internal hiring process that evaluated candidates across technical aptitude, leadership experience, and familiarity with MEG's operational environment. The selection committee included the COO, IT Director, and an external cybersecurity advisor.

The IT Department supports cybersecurity operations under the direction of Sarah Chen, IT Director, who oversees the department budget, vendor relationships, and strategic technology initiatives. James Thompson serves as IT Security Manager and manages day-to-day security operations including SIEM monitoring, vulnerability scanning, and access control administration. Alex Rivera, Network Administrator, handles network operations, firewall rule management, and switch/router configuration. Lisa Wong, Help Desk Supervisor, manages endpoint provisioning, user access requests, and desktop support for the facility's 47 workstations and 12 laptops.

Personnel assignments are maintained in MEG's Human Resources Information System (HRIS) and updated within five business days of any personnel change. The IT Director conducts annual role reviews to ensure cybersecurity responsibilities are appropriately distributed across the team.
The CySO reports to the COO. The IT Director handles technical execution. The CySO coordinates with other departments as needed for cybersecurity matters, including Operations, Facilities, and Legal.

The CySO can be reached during business hours at the office number listed above. After-hours, the facility operations center can relay urgent messages to the CySO or IT Security Manager. Response times vary based on the nature of the request and staff availability.

The organizational chart is reviewed annually by the COO and IT Director to ensure cybersecurity roles and responsibilities remain aligned with facility operations. Any changes to the reporting structure are documented in the CSP amendment log and communicated to affected personnel within 10 business days. The most recent organizational review was completed in February 2026 with no changes to the cybersecurity reporting chain.

blocks.text: Jordan Kim was previously employed as IT Security Manager at MEG Westport for four years and brings domain knowledge of existing IT and OT systems, operational workflows, and facility-specific risk factors. Jordan holds CISSP and GICSP certifications.

CySO qualifications per 101.625(e): Jordan Kim demonstrates general knowledge across all 12 required areas. Facility operations and conditions: four years on site at MEG Westport. General cybersecurity guidance and best practices: CISSP. Cyber Incident Response Plan and Cybersecurity Plan: authored both, exercised annually. Cybersecurity equipment and systems: GICSP plus vendor training from Palo Alto Networks, Splunk, and Siemens. Audit, inspection, control, and monitoring methods: led the 2025 internal CSP audit. Relevant laws and regulations: MTSA and 33 CFR Subchapter H coursework. Instruction techniques: delivers the quarterly all-hands awareness briefing. SSI handling and security related communications: 49 CFR part 1520 training completed. Current threat patterns and KEVs: subscribes to the CISA KEV catalog and Siemens ProductCERT feeds. Behavioral threat recognition: insider threat module completed with the FSO. Drills and exercises: conducts and assesses the annual exercise required by 101.635.

In the event the primary CySO is unavailable due to leave, incapacitation, or inability to perform duties, the following alternate is designated as permitted by the definition of Cybersecurity Officer at 101.615: James Thompson, IT Security Manager, 555-0121. Qualifications: CISSP, 12 years IT security experience, OT awareness training completed. Per 101.615, references to the CySO in this Plan apply to the alternate when acting.
The following personnel exercise cybersecurity duties per 101.620(b)(2):

items: CEO Jennifer Morrison to COO David Park to CySO Jordan Kim.
CySO to IT Director Sarah Chen (technical execution).
CySO coordinates with FSO Robert Williams (MTSA coordination, joint incident response).
CySO to CLO Amanda Foster (legal/regulatory, SSI handling).

blocks.text: The CySO is accessible 24 hours per day, 7 days per week, 365 days per year, and the means of contact at any time are identified above, as required by 101.620(b)(3). After-hours contact is maintained through the facility's 24/7 operations center, which has procedures to reach the on-call CySO within 15 minutes.

COTP notification procedures for CySO changes: per 101.630(e)(4), if the CySO changes, MEG will notify USCG Sector Puget Sound via the Sector Command Center as soon as reasonably practicable in light of the individual circumstances and in no case longer than 96 hours. The affected portion of this Plan will be amended and submitted to the Coast Guard for review and approval on the same standard, as soon as reasonably practicable and in no case longer than 96 hours. The 30-day advance submission at 101.630(e)(2) governs proposed amendments generally and does not apply to a change of CySO. MEG serves no other facility under this CySO designation; if that changes, each covered facility will be listed in this Plan per 101.625(b).

gap_analysis.intro: The strengthened draft closes each of the gaps below that the original draft left open.

regulatory_gaps.title: No 24/7 availability
regulatory_gaps.explanation: 101.620(b)(3) requires the owner or operator to designate a CySO who is accessible to the Coast Guard 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and to identify how the CySO can be contacted at any time. The deficient draft limits availability to business hours with after-hours message relay, which does not meet the requirement.

regulatory_gaps.title: No mobile or emergency contact
regulatory_gaps.explanation: 101.620(b)(3) requires the plan to identify how the CySO can be contacted at any time. The deficient draft lists only an office number and an email address. The compliant draft adds a 24/7 mobile number and an emergency line with an on-call protocol.

best_practice_improvements.title: 12 knowledge areas not demonstrated
best_practice_improvements.explanation: There is no requirement to reproduce the CySO's resume in the CSP. However, 101.625(e) requires the CySO to have general knowledge, through training, education, or equivalent job experience, across 12 specific areas: facility operations and conditions; general cybersecurity guidance and best practices; the Cyber Incident Response Plan; the Cybersecurity Plan; cybersecurity equipment and systems; methods of conducting cybersecurity audits, inspections, control, and monitoring; relevant laws and regulations; instruction techniques for cybersecurity training and education; handling of Sensitive Security Information and security related communications; current cybersecurity threat patterns and KEVs; recognizing characteristics and behavioral patterns of persons likely to threaten security; and conducting and assessing cybersecurity drills and exercises. The compliant draft maps each area to evidence of competency. The deficient draft cites vendor training and certifications without addressing the required areas, and never touches SSI handling, behavioral threat recognition, or drills and exercises.

best_practice_improvements.title: No FSO coordination relationship documented
best_practice_improvements.explanation: While the regulation does not explicitly require listing the FSO in the CySO section, 101.620(b)(2) requires the owner or operator to define the cybersecurity organizational structure and identify each person exercising cybersecurity duties and responsibilities within that structure, with the support needed to fulfill those obligations. Documenting the CySO-FSO coordination relationship, joint incident response responsibilities, and CSP/FSP integration points is a best practice that strengthens the plan. The compliant draft names the FSO and defines the coordination relationship. The deficient draft does not mention the FSO at all.

best_practice_improvements.title: No alternate CySO designated
best_practice_improvements.explanation: An alternate CySO is not mandatory. The definition of Cybersecurity Officer at 101.615 provides that the owner or operator may designate an alternate CySO to assist with the duties and responsibilities of the CySO, including during periods when the CySO is on leave, unavailable, or unable to perform their duties, and that the term CySO thereafter refers to both. Given the 24/7 accessibility requirement at 101.620(b)(3), designating an alternate is a practical way to sustain coverage. The compliant draft designates one. The deficient draft omits this entirely.

blocks.text: MEG uses Microsoft 365 (Exchange Online, SharePoint, Teams) to communicate cybersecurity information to personnel. The CySO sends email updates to IT staff distribution lists when cybersecurity conditions change. Phone calls are used for urgent matters via the facility PBX system. The facility has a PA announcement system in Building 1, Building 3, and the Operations Control Center for building-wide notifications.

MEG's Microsoft 365 E3 licensing provides enterprise-grade email security, including Microsoft Defender for Office 365 with anti-phishing, safe attachments, and safe links. Email retention policies are configured for 7-year retention in compliance with records management requirements.

Cybersecurity incidents are reported to the CySO, who determines the appropriate response based on the nature and scope of the event. For serious incidents, the CySO notifies the COO. The IT Director is consulted on technical matters as needed. All escalation decisions are documented in the incident tracking system for post-incident review.

MEG maintains backup communication capabilities through the facility's Veeam backup infrastructure. Critical communication systems including Exchange Online and SharePoint are backed up daily with incremental snapshots. Full backups are performed weekly and stored on the Dell PowerEdge R740 backup server. In the event of a communication system failure, IT can restore email services within 4 hours using the most recent backup. Backup integrity is verified through automated checksum validation.

MEG will contact the Coast Guard and other authorities as required in the event of a significant cybersecurity incident. Contact information for relevant agencies is maintained by the CySO in a secure document stored on the facility SharePoint site. The CySO updates this contact list annually during the CSP review cycle to ensure accuracy.
Per 101.645(a), the CySO maintains the following means to notify owners, operators, and all personnel of changes in cybersecurity conditions:

items: Email via Microsoft 365 distribution lists (all-hands, IT staff, OT operators, management).
Telephone: Facility main number 555-0100, CySO direct 555-0190, Operations Center 555-0110.
VHF Marine Radio: Channel 16 (emergency) and Channel 13 (vessel-to-shore operations).
In-person briefings at Operations Control Center (Building 3) for shift-change security updates.
SMS/text alert system via facility emergency notification system for time-critical alerts.
Satellite phone for communication with MEG-1 platform (555-0161) and vessels at sea.

gap_analysis.intro: The strengthened draft closes each of the gaps below that the original draft left open.

regulatory_gaps.title: No specific authority contact information
regulatory_gaps.explanation: The regulation requires effective and continuous communications with COTP and other authorities. The deficient draft vaguely states that contact information is maintained without listing specific agencies or numbers (NRC, CISA, FBI).

regulatory_gaps.title: No personnel notification for cybersecurity condition changes
regulatory_gaps.explanation: 101.645(a) explicitly requires means to notify all personnel of changes in cybersecurity conditions. The compliant draft specifies multiple channels for notifying all personnel (email lists, SMS alerts, in-person briefings, shift-change updates). The deficient draft only mentions IT staff email updates.

best_practice_improvements.title: No out-of-band communication plan
best_practice_improvements.explanation: The regulation requires means to notify personnel but does not specifically mandate backup channels for when primary systems are compromised. However, establishing out-of-band communication (VHF, satellite, physical runner) is a best practice that ensures the facility can maintain notification capability during a cyber incident affecting email and VoIP.

best_practice_improvements.title: No severity-based escalation with timelines
best_practice_improvements.explanation: 101.645(a) requires a means to notify personnel of changes in cybersecurity conditions but does not mandate a tiered severity matrix. Defining severity levels with specific notification chains and internal timelines is a best practice that produces consistent response. Note that the regulation's own reporting obligation is not a tiered timeline at all: 101.650(g)(1) requires reportable cyber incidents to be reported to the NRC without delay, and that obligation is documented in Sections 3 and 9. A facility-defined internal escalation clock must never be read as extending the regulatory one.

best_practice_improvements.title: Backup and recovery content does not belong in Section 5
best_practice_improvements.explanation: Section 5.3 of the original draft discusses Veeam backup infrastructure, restore times, and backup integrity. Backup of critical IT and OT systems is required by 101.650(g)(4), and the lead-in to 101.650(g) places it in Sections 3 and 9 of the Plan. Section 9 is cybersecurity measures for monitoring under 101.630(c)(9). Including it under Communications is a red herring: it looks thorough but does not address the Section 5 requirement for notification means that survive a compromise of the primary systems. Restoring email from backup four hours later is not out-of-band communication capability.

visuals.caption: The strengthened plan defines a severity-tiered escalation chain with timelines, replacing the original draft's single undifferentiated notification path.

checklist.label: Formal risk acceptance with documented justification
KEV patching or compensating controls without delay

blocks.text: MEG tracks known vulnerabilities through a comprehensive scanning program. The IT Security Manager conducts quarterly vulnerability scans using Tenable Nessus Professional (v10.6) across all IT network segments. Nessus is configured with the following scan profiles: a full network scan covering the Corporate IT zone (10.50.0.0/16), DMZ (192.168.1.0/24), and Guest/Temp network (10.30.0.0/24); a credentialed Windows scan for all domain-joined systems using a dedicated scan service account; and a web application scan for internal-facing services.

Scan results are exported to CSV format and reviewed by the IT Security Manager within 5 business days of scan completion. Vulnerabilities are categorized by Nessus severity (Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational) and tracked in a shared Excel spreadsheet on the facility SharePoint site. The spreadsheet includes columns for vulnerability name, affected host, severity, date discovered, assigned owner, and status.

For OT systems, MEG relies on vendor notifications from Siemens ProductCERT and Inductive Automation for vulnerability information, as active scanning of OT networks is not performed due to the risk of disrupting real-time control processes. Thomas Nakamura reviews vendor advisories monthly and coordinates with the IT Security Manager on any patches or firmware updates affecting OT equipment.
When vulnerabilities are identified, the IT team develops remediation plans during the weekly IT staff meeting. Patches for Windows systems are deployed through Microsoft SCCM [SOURCE TRUNCATED]

gap_analysis.intro: The strengthened draft closes each of the gaps below that the original draft left open.

regulatory_gaps.title: No documentation of unresolved vulnerabilities or accepted risk
regulatory_gaps.explanation: 101.630(c)(12) requires the Plan to document all identified, unresolved vulnerabilities, including those that are intentionally unresolved due to owner or operator risk acceptance. The deficient draft describes how vulnerabilities are found and tracked but never establishes what happens to one that will not be fixed. There is no acceptance authority, no written justification, no compensating control, and no review date. A status column in a SharePoint spreadsheet is a tracker, not the risk acceptance record the regulation requires.

regulatory_gaps.title: Remediation cadence cannot meet the without-delay KEV standard
regulatory_gaps.explanation: 101.650(e)(3)(i) requires patching or documented compensating controls for all KEVs in critical IT or OT systems without delay, and 101.625(d)(15) places the same duty on the CySO directly. No day count is specified; the obligation is immediate. The deficient draft routes every finding through quarterly IT scans, monthly OT vendor advisory review, and a weekly IT staff meeting. That cadence can leave a KEV in a critical OT system unaddressed for months and does not satisfy the standard, however well the tracking is documented.

regulatory_gaps.title: No KEV identification source or critical system scoping
regulatory_gaps.explanation: The without-delay obligation applies specifically to KEVs in critical IT or OT systems, so the Plan must show how KEVs are identified and which systems are in scope. The deficient draft categorizes findings by Nessus severity only. Nessus severity is not the KEV catalog: a medium-severity finding can be a KEV, and a critical-severity finding often is not. Without a KEV feed and a designation of critical systems, the facility cannot demonstrate compliance.

regulatory_gaps.title: OT networks are not analyzed, only monitored by vendor advisory
regulatory_gaps.explanation: 101.650(e)(1)(i) requires analysis of all networks to identify vulnerabilities to critical IT and OT systems and the risk posed by each digital asset. The deficient draft declines to scan OT and substitutes monthly review of Siemens ProductCERT and Inductive Automation advisories. Declining to actively scan a live control network is a defensible engineering decision, but it does not discharge the analysis obligation. Passive discovery, configuration review, or an asset inventory with per-asset risk determination is needed, and the reliance on vendor advisories alone leaves any asset outside those two vendors' catalogs unanalyzed.

best_practice_improvements.title: No statement on OT internet exposure or exploitable channels
best_practice_improvements.explanation: 101.650(e)(3)(v) requires that no OT be connected to the publicly accessible internet unless explicitly required for operation, with documented justification for any remotely accessible OT system, and 101.650(e)(3)(iv) requires no exploitable channels directly exposed to internet-accessible systems. These are Section 6 obligations under routine system maintenance, so their absence from Section 12 is not itself a Section 12 defect. However, any remote OT access that is knowingly retained is an accepted risk and belongs in the Section 12 register with its justification. The deficient draft is silent on both.

cfr:101.625(b).text: Serving as CySO for Multiple Vessels, Facilities, or OCS Facilities. The same person may serve as the CySO for more than one U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility. If a person serves as the CySO for more than one U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility, the name of each U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility for which that person is the CySO must be listed in the Cybersecurity Plan of each U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility for which that person is the CySO.

cfr:101.625(d).title: CySO Responsibilities
cfr:101.625(d).description: Does NOT create the alternate CySO. The alternate provision is in the 101.615 definition of Cybersecurity Officer.
cfr:101.625(d).text: Responsibilities. For each U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility for which they are designated, the CySO must ensure the Cybersecurity Assessment is conducted; ensure the cybersecurity measures in the Cybersecurity Plan are developed, implemented, and operating as intended; ensure an annual audit is conducted and the Plan updated if necessary; ensure the Cyber Incident Response Plan is executed and exercised; ensure the Plan is exercised per 101.635(c); arrange for cybersecurity inspections; ensure prompt correction of problems identified by exercises, audits, or inspections; enhance cybersecurity awareness and vigilance of personnel; ensure adequate cybersecurity training; ensure all reportable cyber incidents are recorded and reported to the owner or operator; ensure records are maintained per 101.640; ensure required reports are prepared and submitted; ensure the Plan and proposed amendments are submitted for approval per 101.630; ensure relevant security and management personnel are briefed regarding changes in cybersecurity conditions; and ensure identification and mitigation of all KEVs in critical IT or OT systems, without delay. [Paragraphs (d)(1) through (15), condensed. Individual subparagraphs quoted verbatim where cited.]

cfr:101.625(e).title: CySO Qualifications
cfr:101.625(e).text: Qualifications. The CySO must have general knowledge, through training, education, or equivalent job experience, in the following: (1) General vessel, facility, or OCS facility operations and conditions; (2) General cybersecurity guidance and best practices; (3) The vessel, facility, or OCS facility's Cyber Incident Response Plan; (4) The vessel, facility, or OCS facility's Cybersecurity Plan; (5) Cybersecurity equipment and systems; (6) Methods of conducting cybersecurity audits, inspections, control, and monitoring techniques; (7) Relevant laws and regulations pertaining to cybersecurity; (8) Instruction techniques for cybersecurity training and education; (9) Handling of Sensitive Security Information and security related communications; (10) Current cybersecurity threat patterns and KEVs; (11) Recognizing characteristics and behavioral patterns of persons who are likely to threaten security; and (12) Conducting and assessing cybersecurity drills and exercises.

cfr:101.630(c)(5).title: Communications
cfr:101.630(c)(5).description: Section 5 of the CSP is the communications section.

cfr:101.645(a).title: Notification of cybersecurity condition changes
cfr:101.645(a).text: The CySO must have a means to effectively notify owners or operators and personnel of a U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility of changes in cybersecurity conditions at the U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, and OCS facility and document these means in Section 5 of the Cybersecurity Plan.

cfr:101.645(b).title: Continuous communications with authorities
cfr:101.645(b).text: Communication systems and procedures must allow effective and continuous communications between U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, and OCS facility security personnel, vessels interfacing with a facility or an OCS facility, the cognizant COTP, and national and local authorities with security responsibilities.

cfr:101.650(g).title: Resilience
cfr:101.650(g).description: Resilience, not incident reporting timelines. Note that (g) is documented in Sections 3 and 9, not Section 5.
cfr:101.650(g).text: Resilience. Each owner or operator or designated CySO of a U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility must ensure the following measures for resilience are in place and documented in Sections 3 and 9 of the Cybersecurity Plan: (1) For entities that have not reported to the Coast Guard pursuant to, or not subject to, 33 CFR 6.16-1, report reportable cyber incidents to the NRC without delay; (2) In addition to other plans mentioned in this subpart, develop, implement, maintain, and exercise the Cyber Incident Response Plan; (3) Periodically validate the effectiveness of the Cybersecurity Plan through annual exercises, annual reviews of incident response cases, or post-cyber incident review, as determined by the owner or operator; and (4) Perform backup of critical IT and OT systems, with those backups being sufficiently protected and tested frequently.

cfr:101.630(c)(12).title: Documentation of Unresolved Vulnerabilities
cfr:101.630(c)(12).description: Section 12 documents all identified, unresolved vulnerabilities, including any intentionally accepted risk.
cfr:101.630(c)(12).text: Documentation of all identified, unresolved vulnerabilities, to include those that are intentionally unresolved due to owner or operator risk acceptance.

cfr:101.650(e)(3)(i).title: KEV patching without delay
cfr:101.650(e)(3)(i).description: Sits under 101.650(e)(3) Routine system maintenance, which is documented in Section 6 of the Cybersecurity Plan. The parallel CySO duty is 101.625(d)(15).
cfr:101.650(e)(3)(i).text: Ensure patching or implementation of documented compensating controls for all KEVs in critical IT or OT systems, without delay;

cfr:101.625(d)(15).title: CySO duty to mitigate KEVs without delay
cfr:101.625(d)(15).text: Ensure identification and mitigation of all KEVs in critical IT or OT systems, without delay.

cfr:101.615.title: Definition: Cybersecurity Officer (CySO)
cfr:101.615.description: This definition, not 101.625(d), is the source of the alternate CySO provision.
cfr:101.615.text: Cybersecurity Officer, or CySO, means the person designated as responsible for the development, implementation, and maintenance of the cybersecurity portions of the Vessel Security Plan (VSP), Facility Security Plan (FSP), or Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) FSP, and for liaison with the Captain of the Port (COTP) and Company, Vessel, and Facility Security Officers. The owner or operator may designate an alternate CySO(s) to assist with the duties and responsibilities of the CySO, including during periods when the CySO is on leave, unavailable, or unable to perform their duties. Hereafter, “CySO” will refer to both the CySO and the alternate CySO(s), as applicable.

cfr:101.630(c)(11).title: Reports of audits and inspections
cfr:101.630(c)(11).description: Section 11 holds resolved findings. Section 12 holds what remains unresolved.
cfr:101.630(c)(11).text: Reports of all cybersecurity audits and inspections, to include documentation of resolution or mitigation of all identified vulnerabilities;

cfr:101.650(g)(4).title: Backup of critical IT and OT systems
cfr:101.650(g)(4).description: Documented in Sections 3 and 9 of the Cybersecurity Plan, per the lead-in to 101.650(g).
cfr:101.650(g)(4).text: Perform backup of critical IT and OT systems, with those backups being sufficiently protected and tested frequently.

cfr:101.650(e)(1)(i).title: Analyze all networks for vulnerabilities
cfr:101.650(e)(1)(i).text: Analyze all networks to identify vulnerabilities to critical IT and OT systems and the risk posed by each digital asset;

cfr:101.650(e)(3)(iv).title: No exploitable channels exposed to internet
cfr:101.650(e)(3)(iv).text: Ensure there are no exploitable channels directly exposed to internet-accessible systems;

cfr:101.650(e)(3)(v).title: OT internet exposure requires documented justification
cfr:101.650(e)(3)(v).text: Ensure no OT is connected to the publicly accessible internet unless explicitly required for operation, and verify that, for any remotely accessible OT system, there is a documented justification; and

cfr:101.650(e)(3)(vi).title: Vulnerability scans as specified in the Plan
cfr:101.650(e)(3)(vi).text: Conduct vulnerability scans as specified in the Cybersecurity Plan.

cfr:101.630(e)(2).title: Amendments: 30-day advance submission
cfr:101.630(e)(2).description: The general amendment rule. It does NOT govern a change of CySO, which is 101.630(e)(4).
cfr:101.630(e)(2).text: Proposed amendments to the Cybersecurity Plan must be sent to the Coast Guard at least 30 days before the proposed amendment's effective date. The Coast Guard will approve or disapprove the proposed amendment in accordance with this part.

cfr:101.630(e)(4).title: CySO change: 96 hours to notify and 96 hours to submit
cfr:101.630(e)(4).description: Two separate 96-hour clocks, notification and submission of the amended portion. The 30-day rule at 101.630(e)(2) does not apply to this case.
cfr:101.630(e)(4).text: If the CySO has changed, the Coast Guard must be notified as soon as reasonably practicable in light of the individual circumstances, but, in any case, not longer than 96 hours, and the affected portion of the Cybersecurity Plan must be amended and submitted to the Coast Guard for review and approval in accordance with this part as soon as reasonably practicable in light of the individual circumstances, but, in any case, not longer than 96 hours.

cfr:101.650(a).title: Account security measures (Section 7)
cfr:101.650(a).description: Lead-in only. The subparagraph obligations are cited individually.
cfr:101.650(a).text: Account security measures. Each owner or operator of a U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility must ensure, at a minimum, the following account security measures are in place and documented in Section 7 of the Cybersecurity Plan:

cfr:101.650(b).title: Device security measures (Section 6)
cfr:101.650(b).description: Lead-in only. The subparagraph obligations are cited individually.
cfr:101.650(b).text: Device security measures. Each owner or operator or designated CySO of a U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility must ensure the following device security measures are in place, addressed in Section 6 of the Cybersecurity Plan, and made available to the Coast Guard upon request:

cfr:101.650(c).title: Data security measures (Section 4)
cfr:101.650(c).description: Lead-in only. The subparagraph obligations are cited individually.
cfr:101.650(c).text: Data security measures. Each owner or operator or designated CySO of a U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility must ensure the following data security measures are in place and documented in Section 4 of the Cybersecurity Plan:

cfr:101.650(d).title: Cybersecurity training for personnel (Sections 2 and 4)
cfr:101.650(d).description: Lead-in only. The subparagraph obligations are cited individually.
cfr:101.650(d).text: Cybersecurity training for personnel. The training program to address requirements under this paragraph must be documented in Sections 2 and 4 of the Cybersecurity Plan.

cfr:101.650(e).title: Risk management (Sections 11 and 12)
cfr:101.650(e).description: Lead-in only. The subparagraph obligations are cited individually.
cfr:101.650(e).text: Risk management. Each owner or operator or designated CySO of a U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility must ensure the following measures for risk management are in place and documented in Sections 11 and 12 of the Cybersecurity Plan:

cfr:101.650(e)(3).title: Routine system maintenance (Section 6)
cfr:101.650(e)(3).description: Lead-in only. The subparagraph obligations are cited individually.
cfr:101.650(e)(3).text: Routine system maintenance. Each owner or operator or a designated CySO of a U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility must ensure the following measures for routine system maintenance are in place and documented in Section 6 of the Cybersecurity Plan:

cfr:101.650(f).title: Supply chain (Section 4)
cfr:101.650(f).description: Lead-in only. The subparagraph obligations are cited individually.
cfr:101.650(f).text: Supply chain. Each owner or operator or designated CySO of a U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility must ensure the following supply-chain measures are in place and documented in Section 4 of the Cybersecurity Plan:

cfr:101.650(h).title: Network segmentation (Sections 7 and 8)
cfr:101.650(h).description: Lead-in only. The subparagraph obligations are cited individually.
cfr:101.650(h).text: Network segmentation. Each owner or operator or designated CySO of a U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility must ensure the following measures for network segmentation are in place and documented in Sections 7 and 8 of the Cybersecurity Plan:

cfr:101.650(i).title: Physical security (Sections 7 and 8)
cfr:101.650(i).description: Lead-in only. The subparagraph obligations are cited individually.
cfr:101.650(i).text: Physical security. Each owner, operator, or designated CySO of a U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, or OCS facility must ensure the following measures for physical security are in place and documented in Sections 7 and 8 of the Cybersecurity Plan:

cfr:101.620(b)(7).title: Owner or operator duty to report to the NRC
cfr:101.620(b)(7).text: For entities that have not reported to the Coast Guard pursuant to, or are not subject to, 33 CFR 6.16-1, ensure all reportable cyber incidents are reported to the National Response Center (NRC).

cfr:101.635.title: Drills and exercises
cfr:101.635.description: Section 3 of the Plan. The 2 drills, 1 exercise, and 18-month ceiling are (b)(1) and (c)(1).
cfr:101.635.text: Drills and exercises must be used to test the proficiency of the U.S.-flagged vessel, facility, and OCS facility personnel in assigned cybersecurity duties and the effective implementation of the VSP, FSP, OCS FSP, and Cybersecurity Plan. Drills must be conducted at least twice each calendar year. Exercises must be conducted at least once each calendar year, with no more than 18 months between exercises. Each exercise must test communication and notification procedures and elements of coordination, resource availability, and response, and must include the substantial and active participation of the CySO(s). [101.635(a) through (c), condensed. Individual paragraphs quoted verbatim where cited.]

cfr:101.640.title: Records and documentation
cfr:101.640.description: Defines no retention period of its own. It defers to 104.235, 105.225, and 106.230, all outside Subpart F.
cfr:101.640.text: All records, reports, and other documents mentioned in this subpart must be created and maintained in accordance with 33 CFR 104.235 for U.S.-flagged vessels, 105.225 for facilities, and 106.230 for OCS facilities. At a minimum, the records must be created for the following activities: training, drills, exercises, cybersecurity threats, reportable cyber incidents, and audits of the Cybersecurity Plan.

cfr:101.630(f).title: Audits
cfr:101.630(f).description: Auditor independence is (f)(4). The 30-day post-audit amendment clock is (f)(5).
cfr:101.630(f).text: The CySO must ensure that an audit of the Cybersecurity Plan and its implementation is performed annually, beginning no later than 1 year from the initial date of approval, and must attach a report to the Plan certifying that the Plan meets the applicable requirements of this subpart. An additional audit is required if there is a change in the owner or operator or if there have been modifications to the cybersecurity measures. Personnel conducting internal audits must have knowledge of audit methods, must not have regularly assigned cybersecurity duties for the entity being audited, and must be independent of any cybersecurity measures being audited. If an audit requires amending the Plan, the amendments must be submitted no later than 30 days after completion of the audit. [101.630(f)(1) through (5), condensed.]

cfr:101.630(d).title: Submission and approval
cfr:101.630(d).description: Multi-facility plans are (d)(2). The 5-year validity is (d)(3).
cfr:101.630(d).text: Each owner or operator must submit one copy of their Cybersecurity Plan for review and approval to the cognizant COTP or the OCMI for a facility or OCS facility, or to the MSC for a U.S.-flagged vessel. Owners or operators submitting one Cybersecurity Plan to cover two or more U.S.-flagged vessels, facilities, or OCS facilities of similar operations must ensure the Plan addresses the specific cybersecurity risks for each. A Plan that is approved by the COTP, OCMI, or MSC is valid for 5 years from the date of its approval. [101.630(d)(1) through (3), condensed.]
